method: Suggested experience is editorial browsing guidance based on the lesson's own prerequisites, setup, and inputs. sourceExcerpt quotes the visible lesson body, and sourceHeading identifies its section. Study order and learning format do not prove execution or validation.

computer-data-fundamentals.prerequisiteSummary: Requires a Bash-capable terminal on macOS, Linux, or WSL; internet is optional for examples, and no programming experience is needed.
computer-data-fundamentals.sourceHeading: What you will produce and what you need
computer-data-fundamentals.sourceExcerpt: No prior programming experience is required; the lesson focuses on concepts and safe command usage.

biological-data-formats.prerequisiteSummary: Basic shell familiarity is needed for the inspection commands; bring your own files, since no dataset is bundled.
biological-data-formats.sourceExcerpt: Run these from a directory containing your own inputs, or replace each name with its path. The commands below do not overwrite input files.

quality-control-fundamentals.prerequisiteSummary: Know basic shell commands and paths, and complete the biological-formats introduction; actual QC runs additionally need FASTQ, provider checksums, references, and installed tools.
quality-control-fundamentals.sourceExcerpt: Familiarity with command-line basics and file paths. Completed an introduction to biological data formats (FASTQ, BAM/CRAM, VCF, gene-count matrices). Thresholds depend on assay, organism, library protocol, instrument, and study design.

git-github-bioinformatics.prerequisiteSummary: Have a terminal, Git, and Python 3 available for the later script; a GitHub account and remote are optional, and examples are data-free.
git-github-bioinformatics.sourceExcerpt: You need a terminal, Git, and Python 3 for the later script and provenance sections. Check that Git and Python are available; the pip check confirms the Python package manager if you choose the optional package inventory step:

python-fundamentals-bioinformatics.prerequisiteSummary: Bring basic command-line and editor familiarity, Python 3.10 or newer, and a POSIX shell; the small FASTA input is supplied as fixture text.
python-fundamentals-bioinformatics.sourceExcerpt: Python 3.10 or newer installed. This lesson uses explicit commands for Python 3; adjust to your system's python executable if needed.

r-tidyverse-fundamentals.prerequisiteSummary: Basic file and command-line skills plus an R session with the required packages are needed; package installation can require build prerequisites, network, and writable library.
r-tidyverse-fundamentals.sourceHeading: Check the package setup before running the lab
r-tidyverse-fundamentals.sourceExcerpt: Downloads and source compilation can take time; do not continue past an installation error. If the packages already load in a suitable managed environment, skip installation but run the readiness check there and keep using that environment.

statistics-for-bioinformatics.prerequisiteSummary: Understand independent biological units and two-group comparisons; Python execution needs Python 3, NumPy, pandas, and SciPy, while the base-R route uses no add-on packages.
statistics-for-bioinformatics.sourceExcerpt: For Python, use Python 3 and install NumPy, pandas, and SciPy 1.11 or newer in an environment you manage;

experimental-design-batch-effects.prerequisiteSummary: Know biological units, conditions, and sample metadata; running the PCA requires a count matrix plus validated metadata, with Python/pandas or base R available.
experimental-design-batch-effects.sourceExcerpt: The experimental unit is the unit independently assigned to a treatment or condition. It is often a participant, animal, culture, or independently prepared sample. Repeated measurements from one unit and technical replicates do not create additional independent biological replicates.

reference-genomes-annotation.prerequisiteSummary: Have basic POSIX-shell familiarity and substantial disk space/time; select a species-appropriate assembly and matching annotation, and use samtools for FASTA indexing.
reference-genomes-annotation.sourceExcerpt: The commands below have not been run against the full human reference files in this review. Large reference downloads require substantial disk space and time.

data-visualization-fundamentals.prerequisiteSummary: Basic Python and tabular-data familiarity are needed for synthetic QC, PCA, UMAP, and heatmap examples; the separate volcano plot also needs R and ggplot2.
data-visualization-fundamentals.sourceHeading: Start with the question and the data contract
data-visualization-fundamentals.sourceExcerpt: Choose a plot to answer a defined question. Distributions help compare per-sample QC metrics; PCA summarizes major linear variation among samples; UMAP emphasizes neighborhood structure in a chosen feature space; a heatmap displays selected values across genes and samples; and a volcano plot combines an effect estimate with an adjusted significance measure from a differential-expression analysis.

reproducible-project-structure.prerequisiteSummary: Requires basic Bash and Git on a Unix-like shell; optional Conda, pip, or R/renv examples also require those managers and are not needed for scaffold.
reproducible-project-structure.sourceExcerpt: By the end, you can create a role-oriented project tree, record checksums and software versions, and prepare a run wrapper that logs its code revision and configuration path. You will also know what these records can and cannot establish.

research-reporting-interpretation.prerequisiteSummary: Bring a plot or small analysis result, basic command-line familiarity, and a Git repository; prior data visualization experience is required or must be equivalent.
research-reporting-interpretation.sourceExcerpt: Completed "Data Visualization Fundamentals" or equivalent experience creating and exporting at least one plot. A small analysis result or QC plot to describe (for example: a per-sample QC table and one summary plot).

introduction-to-bioinformatics.prerequisiteSummary: No data or software setup is needed to complete the question-to-method planning exercise; learners should be ready to identify inputs and design assumptions.
introduction-to-bioinformatics.sourceExcerpt: A computational analysis is useful when its inputs and comparisons match a question that can be answered by the available experiment. “Which genes differ in expression between these conditions?” calls for an expression study with appropriate biological replicates and a design that records relevant covariates.

modern-bioinformatics-methods-2026.prerequisiteSummary: Bring a study plan or hypothetical scenario and understand observation units, replicate structure, data modalities, and input contracts; no dataset or runnable pipeline is supplied.
modern-bioinformatics-methods-2026.sourceExcerpt: Write down the unit of observation and the unit of replication before choosing software. A cell is an observation; in a condition comparison, the biological sample or donor is commonly the independent replicate.

command-line-part1.prerequisiteSummary: Use a working terminal on Linux, macOS, or WSL; copy/paste familiarity helps, but no shell experience is required.
command-line-part1.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites: a working terminal on Linux, macOS, or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). No prior shell experience required, but basic familiarity with copying and pasting text will help.

command-line-part2.prerequisiteSummary: Requires basic shell navigation, Bash, standard text utilities, and SeqKit for sequence-aware exercises; use a fresh practice directory rather than research data.
command-line-part2.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites: Basic shell navigation, a Bash terminal, the usual text utilities, and SeqKit. Start in a fresh practice directory, not a directory containing research data: the setup writes the five named teaching files.

command-line-part3.prerequisiteSummary: Be comfortable with shell navigation and Bash scripts; the lesson uses standard utilities and synthetic FASTQ/annotation fixtures, with no Python, R, or SeqKit needed.
command-line-part3.sourceExcerpt: It does not call SeqKit, R, or Python, so no additional packages are needed here. SeqKit is used for the sequence-aware steps in Part 2.

conda-mamba-part1.prerequisiteSummary: Have a Bash terminal and permission to create files and install packages in a user-owned location; Micromamba setup may be needed before the lab.
conda-mamba-part1.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites: A Bash terminal and permission to create files and install packages in a user-owned location. If Micromamba is not installed yet, use the installation section below first; Windows PowerShell has separately labeled installation instructions.

hpc-connection.prerequisiteSummary: For hands-on login, obtain an authorized cluster account, exact hostname, and institutional access instructions; without access, only planning and symptom checks are possible.
hpc-connection.sourceExcerpt: You need a cluster username, the exact login hostname, and permission to access the system. Ask the HPC support team whether you must connect through a VPN or bastion host, whether keys are accepted, how to register a key, and which host is intended for interactive login.

hpc-basic-commands.prerequisiteSummary: Requires basic shell commands, SSH access to a Slurm account, and the cluster's current documentation; Python 3 is only needed for the local smoke test.
hpc-basic-commands.sourceExcerpt: This reference is for learners who already know basic shell commands and have an account with SSH access to a Slurm cluster. Work from the login node only for setup and submission, not for compute work.

hpc-submission-part1.prerequisiteSummary: Complete Basic Slurm Commands first, obtain an authorized account and site-specific partition/resource details, and understand the harmless test before submitting jobs.
hpc-submission-part1.sourceExcerpt: Complete the preceding Basic Slurm Commands lesson. Check your cluster's account, allowed partition, time limit, output-file location, and submission rules. Add an account directive only if your site requires one.

hpc-support.prerequisiteSummary: Bring cluster access, a job ID, original script or command, and logs; basic shell skills plus familiarity with the site's environment system and job tools are assumed.
hpc-support.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites: you have access to the cluster where your jobs ran, the original submission script or command, and the job ID(s) you want to investigate. Familiarity with basic shell commands, your cluster's module or environment system (Modules or Conda), and the bioinformatics tool(s) used in the job is assumed.

reproducible-workflows-snakemake-nextflo.prerequisiteSummary: Know shell commands, paths, and input-to-output dependencies; install either Snakemake or Nextflow in an isolated environment, with supported Java needed for Nextflow examples.
reproducible-workflows-snakemake-nextflo.sourceExcerpt: Write down each step as an input-to-output contract before choosing a workflow manager. For a two-step analysis, the contract might be: raw reads plus a reference produce an alignment; the alignment plus an annotation produce a count table.

docker-singularity-bioinformatics.prerequisiteSummary: Requires terminal comfort, Docker daemon access, and host-side BWA for the local runnable exercise; the optional Slurm section needs authorized cluster access and Apptainer.
docker-singularity-bioinformatics.sourceHeading: Prepare a small, explicit project layout
docker-singularity-bioinformatics.sourceExcerpt: The commands require Bash, Docker with permission to access its daemon, and host BWA for indexing. Check availability before starting:

16s-rrna-prokka-annotation.prerequisiteSummary: Begin with the distinction between marker-gene surveys and genome annotation; bring a prepared QIIME 2 artifact or isolate assembly FASTA to adapt the examples.
16s-rrna-prokka-annotation.sourceHeading: Start with the input and question
16s-rrna-prokka-annotation.sourceExcerpt: A feature table is not an assembly. Amplicon profiling targets a selected region of the 16S rRNA gene and does not recover a genome-wide gene catalogue.

metagenomics-assembly-mapping.prerequisiteSummary: Comfort with shell commands and paired-end read QC; prepare matched quality-controlled FASTQ mates, a configured assembler/mapping environment, and a host reference when screening is relevant.
metagenomics-assembly-mapping.sourceHeading: What you need and what you will produce
metagenomics-assembly-mapping.sourceExcerpt: Adapter contamination matters to metaSPAdes, so inspect the upstream QC report before assembly. For host-associated samples, obtain an appropriate host reference FASTA and record its source and checksum.

metagenomics-kraken2-bracken.prerequisiteSummary: Know basic shell and paired FASTQ handling; supply quality-controlled reads, a built Kraken2 database, and Bracken distributions compatible with the intended read length.
metagenomics-kraken2-bracken.sourceHeading: What you need and what you will produce
metagenomics-kraken2-bracken.sourceExcerpt: Prepare quality-controlled paired FASTQ files, a built Kraken2 database, and a compatible Bracken database distribution generated for the read length you intend to analyze.

metatranscriptomics-guide.prerequisiteSummary: Understand microbial RNA-seq as transcript evidence and basic read files; bring paired FASTQs, references, and installed tools to adapt the planning commands.
metatranscriptomics-guide.sourceExcerpt: Inspect raw reads. Run FastQC and aggregate reports with MultiQC. Review per-base quality, adapter content, and overrepresented sequences rather than treating a report score as an automatic pass/fail.

metatranscriptomics-functional-pathways.prerequisiteSummary: Be comfortable with shell and FASTQ processing; bring post-QC, rRNA-depleted reads per sample, metadata, and configured HUMAnN with compatible databases.
metatranscriptomics-functional-pathways.sourceHeading: What you need and what you will produce
metatranscriptomics-functional-pathways.sourceExcerpt: Start with one quality-controlled, rRNA-depleted FASTQ/FASTA file per sample; the run example uses compressed FASTQ. This walkthrough assumes basic shell use plus an installed HUMAnN 3 environment with compatible nucleotide and translated-search databases configured.

evolutionary-phylogeny-analysis.prerequisiteSummary: Prepare homologous sequences in FASTA, understand sequence homology and multiple alignment, and use a Unix-like shell with one selected tree-inference tool.
evolutionary-phylogeny-analysis.sourceExcerpt: Familiarity with biological sequence files (FASTA), basic UNIX command line, and the concept of homologous characters and multiple sequence alignment.

phylogenomics-orthofinder.prerequisiteSummary: Have predicted protein FASTAs for several species and an OrthoFinder run; understand sequence identifiers, proteome completeness, and how orthogroups differ from one-to-one orthologs.
phylogenomics-orthofinder.sourceExcerpt: Before the run, check that each file parses as FASTA, contains protein sequences rather than nucleotide strings, and has at least one record. Check for duplicated headers and truncated or poorly supported gene models.

wes-variant-calling-pipeline.prerequisiteSummary: Use Linux command line and understand FASTQ, BAM, and VCF; obtain paired reads, reference/indexes, capture intervals, and other resources built for the same experiment.
wes-variant-calling-pipeline.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites: Linux command-line experience and familiarity with FASTQ, BAM, and VCF. This is an advanced template, not a bundled-data lab: the example names assume paired-end reads from one sample and a GRCh38 reference; the files are not included. The commands below require resources built for the exact FASTA and capture design, plus adaptation to installed software versions.

scrna-seq-basics.prerequisiteSummary: Be comfortable with Linux, basic R or Python, count matrices and gene IDs, and introductory statistics; install Seurat or Scanpy and its required clustering dependencies.
scrna-seq-basics.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites. You should be comfortable with the Linux command line, basic R or Python, count matrices and gene identifiers, and introductory statistics. Install either Seurat in R or Scanpy in Python before running its script.

scrna-seq-integration-strategies.prerequisiteSummary: Know basic single-cell expression concepts and R/Seurat-style analysis; the lesson supplies public data and scripts, while its diagnostics require careful batch and label interpretation.
scrna-seq-integration-strategies.sourceHeading: 1. Start with a comparison the data can support
scrna-seq-integration-strategies.sourceExcerpt: Why integration is a question, not an obligation. Shared populations make a comparison possible, but an assay label can still be confounded with donor, processing, depth or genuine state. If comparable populations already mix, correction may add little.

scrna-seq-downstream-analysis.prerequisiteSummary: Bring a clustered, annotated single-cell object and understand biological samples as replicates; retain sample metadata and plan a question-specific comparison before choosing tools.
scrna-seq-downstream-analysis.sourceHeading: Start with the biological question and sample design
scrna-seq-downstream-analysis.sourceExcerpt: Before opening a package, write down the comparison you intend to make, the biological replicate, and the evidence that could support or contradict your interpretation. A cell is an observation within a sample; cells from one donor or condition are not independent biological replicates.

scrna-seq-trajectory-inference.prerequisiteSummary: Have a quality-controlled, clustered scRNA-seq object with interpreted markers and a plausible continuous process; be ready to justify representation and root choices.
scrna-seq-trajectory-inference.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites: Complete scRNA-seq Basics, including QC, clustering, and marker interpretation; use data with a plausible continuous process.

transcriptomics-differential-expression.prerequisiteSummary: Bring an annotated Seurat object with raw counts, cell-type labels, condition, and independent sample IDs; understand R objects and sample-level replication.
transcriptomics-differential-expression.sourceExcerpt: Bring: a processed Seurat object with an RNA assay containing raw counts and per-cell metadata for a cell type, a unique biological sample identifier, and condition.

scrna-seq-quality-control.prerequisiteSummary: Have a completed Seurat or AnnData integration object with cell embeddings and batch/sample labels; know how to align metadata and choose representation.
scrna-seq-quality-control.sourceHeading: What you need before calculating scores
scrna-seq-quality-control.sourceExcerpt: This workflow assumes that preprocessing and integration are complete and that you have a saved Seurat object or AnnData file. The object needs a cell-by-dimension embedding and cell-level metadata for the batch or sample label and, when available, a biological annotation.

advanced-visualization-packages.prerequisiteSummary: Complete a basic scRNA-seq workflow including QC, normalization, dimensional reduction, and clustering; use R, Seurat, and ggplot2 for the core exercise.
advanced-visualization-packages.sourceExcerpt: Completed a basic single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) workflow: alignment, count matrix, cell/gene QC, normalization, dimensional reduction and clustering (e.g., using Seurat).

tcr-bcr-repertoire-analysis.prerequisiteSummary: Bring filtered V(D)J contig annotations per sample and the matched Seurat object with sample labels; understand cell barcodes and clone-summary caveats.
tcr-bcr-repertoire-analysis.sourceHeading: What you need and what you will produce
tcr-bcr-repertoire-analysis.sourceExcerpt: Use one filtered contig-annotation CSV per sample, produced by a compatible V(D)J workflow, plus a Seurat object containing the corresponding cells and a sample label in its metadata.

cell-cell-communication.prerequisiteSummary: Have working R and Seurat knowledge plus a processed object with normalized expression and annotated cell identities; retain sample, condition, and batch metadata.
cell-cell-communication.sourceExcerpt: It assumes working knowledge of R and Seurat, and compatible versions of Seurat, LIANA, and dplyr.

cell-type-annotation-methods.prerequisiteSummary: Use basic R and single-cell concepts with the supplied public PBMC reference/query package; compare labels with original RNA markers rather than treating calls as truth.
cell-type-annotation-methods.sourceHeading: 1. Use a real query and a separate reference
cell-type-annotation-methods.sourceExcerpt: This is a compact, label-stratified teaching sample, not an estimate of natural blood-cell proportions

advanced-ai-single-cell.prerequisiteSummary: Know Python and AnnData; provide an authorized human immune-cell H5AD query with documented raw counts and gene symbols, then evaluate model/reference fit and uncertain labels.
advanced-ai-single-cell.sourceHeading: Choose a method by its input and comparison
advanced-ai-single-cell.sourceExcerpt: These methods do not share one interchangeable “AI annotation” interface. CellTypist is a logistic-regression classifier with downloadable or custom models. SingleR transfers labels by comparing query expression with a labeled reference.

infercnv-copy-number-variation.prerequisiteSummary: Complete scRNA-seq QC, normalization, integration, clustering, and cell annotation; use R and prepare filtered raw counts, annotations, and assembly-matched gene coordinates.
infercnv-copy-number-variation.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites: Completed basic single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) workflows: quality control, normalization, integration, clustering, and cell-type annotation.

single-cell-deconvolution.prerequisiteSummary: Bring bulk gene-expression counts and a prepared annotated single-cell reference with cell types and donor IDs; understand reference-based estimates and their limitations.
single-cell-deconvolution.sourceExcerpt: You need bulk gene-expression measurements and a single-cell reference with gene counts, cell-type labels, and donor/sample IDs. The code below is an analysis scaffold: replace the named objects and metadata fields with your data, and verify package versions and preprocessing before running it.

cite-seq-wnn-multiomics.prerequisiteSummary: Know single-cell RNA-seq and R; prepare matched RNA and ADT count matrices from the same cells and install compatible Seurat before building the WNN object.
cite-seq-wnn-multiomics.sourceExcerpt: Familiarity with single-cell RNA-seq and R. The function names below follow Seurat v4.3 and the current Seurat reference; check the installed version if an argument or object accessor differs.

spatial-transcriptomics-r-python.prerequisiteSummary: Be able to use R or Python; prepare conventional Visium Space Ranger matrix and spatial assets or retrieve the public sample, then inspect spot-image alignment.
spatial-transcriptomics-r-python.sourceHeading: Prepare one public sample for both languages
spatial-transcriptomics-r-python.sourceExcerpt: It downloads approximately 30 MB from 10x Genomics, checks recorded SHA256 fingerprints and stages the mouse-brain H5 matrix and images together.

long-read-pacbio-nanopore.prerequisiteSummary: Know whether the question concerns genomic DNA or long RNA; identify platform/read mode, matched genome/annotation and QC evidence to plan an analysis route.
long-read-pacbio-nanopore.sourceHeading: Start with the molecule and question
long-read-pacbio-nanopore.sourceExcerpt: For genomic DNA, decide whether you need a de novo assembly, read-to-reference structural-variant analysis, or small-variant analysis. For long RNA, decide whether you need transcript structure discovery, transcript abundance, or both.

ai-bioinformatics-github-copilot.prerequisiteSummary: Have a personal GitHub account with current eligible-enrollment evidence, basic terminal familiarity, and Visual Studio Code, Git, and Python 3 for the synthetic review exercise.
ai-bioinformatics-github-copilot.sourceExcerpt: A personal GitHub account and evidence of current enrollment in an eligible degree- or diploma-granting program. Visual Studio Code, Git, and Python 3 for the local practice exercise.

ai-coding-cursor-aider.prerequisiteSummary: Be comfortable with a terminal and Git repositories, local commits, and diffs; have Git and Python 3. Live Cursor/Aider use is optional and needs separately chosen provider access.
ai-coding-cursor-aider.sourceHeading: Keep the assistant inside a reviewable project
ai-coding-cursor-aider.sourceExcerpt: Git must be configured to make a local commit; if it is not, use Git's local repository identity instructions and a placeholder identity for this disposable fixture rather than changing global settings.

mcp-zotero.prerequisiteSummary: Bring a Zotero library or disposable collection and the documentation for the particular MCP server; be ready to assess its permissions, access path, and data flow.
mcp-zotero.sourceExcerpt: Open the project's current README and release information. Confirm its package or repository identity, supported Zotero access method, prerequisites, installation command, and whether it is maintained.

notebooklm-research-brain.prerequisiteSummary: Have two methods papers or protocols you are permitted to process, plus a supported signed-in Google Account for live use and enough source metadata to keep a manifest.
notebooklm-research-brain.sourceHeading: Define the question and source set
notebooklm-research-brain.sourceExcerpt: Choose documents you are permitted to process in a cloud service. Keep an external source manifest with each document’s title, version or publication date, stable URL or identifier, and the question it informs.

deterministic-retrieval-gget-ai.prerequisiteSummary: Know basic Unix-like shell use and how to work in a Python environment; internet access and permission to install Python packages are needed for the retrieval exercise.
deterministic-retrieval-gget-ai.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites: basic command-line familiarity (bash or similar), a Python environment supported by your chosen gget release, and permission to install Python packages.

protein-structure-design-alphafold.prerequisiteSummary: Be able to run basic Python 3.9+ and shell commands; use internet for live retrieval, while local PDB inspection and parser tests can run offline.
protein-structure-design-alphafold.sourceExcerpt: Use Python 3.9 or newer and a shell. The explicit fetch step needs internet access; offline analysis and the included tests do not.

single-cell-foundation-models.prerequisiteSummary: Use Python from a shell and bring externally generated, compatible scGPT or Geneformer vectors with checkpoint/preprocessing provenance, stable cell IDs, labels, and donor metadata.
single-cell-foundation-models.sourceHeading: Model-specific embedding generation handoff (not executed here)
single-cell-foundation-models.sourceExcerpt: Save model/repository revision, checkpoint identifier/hash, tokenizer/vocabulary, organism, input assay/count conventions, preprocessing, cell-ID mapping, embedding layer/pooling, and export date alongside your vectors.

ai-prompt-engineering-seurat.prerequisiteSummary: Know basic scRNA-seq concepts (cells, genes, counts, metadata, clustering, differential expression); prepare compatible AnnData or Seurat objects and R/Python dependencies if running templates.
ai-prompt-engineering-seurat.sourceExcerpt: A generated script and its outputs are not supplied: using an assistant and running either example are optional and require your own compatible input object and software.

autonomous-research-orchestrator.prerequisiteSummary: Know basic Python, CSV files, and terminal commands; Python 3.10+ suffices for offline exercises, while provider setup and model calls are optional.
autonomous-research-orchestrator.sourceExcerpt: Prerequisites: basic Python, CSV files, and terminal commands. Offline path: Python 3.10 or later; no packages, API key, network request, or paid model call is required.

advanced-ai-orchestration-bioinformatics.prerequisiteSummary: Know basic bioinformatics and software-workflow concepts, including how analysis outputs can be independently checked; Python and agent-framework experience, installation, and datasets are not required.
advanced-ai-orchestration-bioinformatics.sourceHeading: Choose the task before choosing agents
advanced-ai-orchestration-bioinformatics.sourceExcerpt: Likewise, an agent can propose steps for a single-cell analysis, but a clustering parameter should not be changed simply because the resulting number of clusters looks unexpected. The analyst must define what counts as an acceptable diagnostic and decide whether a rerun is justified. These are design examples, not reported experiments or validated pipelines.
